synopsis: WAM-OPD adapts an accelerated Flash-WAM student using a frozen LingBot-VA teacher on histories collected by the student. Its central choice is to train action generation under the student's own predicted video, while jointly aligning video and action outputs with teacher targets. Lightweight shared-backbone updates improve reported closed-loop success on two clean RoboTwin tasks. The experiments establish a small adaptation proof of concept; they do not isolate the conditioning mechanism or demonstrate continuously refreshed on-policy learning. [e5, e7, e8, e12, e13, e14]

problem.text: Accelerating a video-first robot policy can leave task-specific capability gaps. Subsequent student errors change its environment histories, while its imperfect video predictions also change the conditions supplied to action generation. Distillation must therefore address both student-induced histories and the student video-to-action interface. The paper studies dense teacher supervision as a way to repair these gaps without sparse-reward policy optimization.

contributions.text: Identifies a conditional mismatch: teacher actions generated under teacher video plans supervise a deployed student whose actions depend on student video plans.
Defines a post-training recipe combining student-plan-conditioned action prediction, video/action endpoint losses, an action flow-matching auxiliary, and shared rank-8 JointLoRA adaptation.
Reports exact-paired improvements on two simulation tasks using the same adaptation configuration. These results evaluate the combined recipe; its individual mechanisms remain unablated.

inputs: Observation–action history and language instruction, h_t = (o_≤t, a_<t, ℓ). [e3]
Released Flash-WAM student and frozen LingBot-VA teacher checkpoints. [e5, e10]
Student-collected histories, teacher video/action targets, and action noise for the flow-matching auxiliary during training. [e5, e6, e8]
outputs: A generated future video-plan latent followed by a conditioned robot action chunk. [e3, e5]
Updated JointLoRA adapters in the student; released backbone weights remain frozen. [e7]

steps.name: Collect student histories
steps.detail: The released student controls environment interaction. The pilot collects one fixed trajectory package, which supplies the histories used for subsequent teacher labeling and optimization.

steps.name: Generate coherent teacher targets
steps.detail: The frozen teacher predicts z_T on each student history and generates a_T conditioned on z_T. It is not queried under the student's exact video plan.

steps.name: Follow the student's deployment computation
steps.detail: The trainable student first generates z_S, then predicts a_S from the history and sg(z_S). Stop-gradient blocks action-loss backpropagation through the plan tensor, while the action forward pass still trains shared adapters.

steps.name: Optimize joint supervision
steps.detail: Pseudo-Huber endpoint penalties align student video and actions with teacher targets. An additional action velocity loss applies at the high-noise boundary. Video alignment is intended to reduce the remaining teacher-plan/student-plan target mismatch.

training.text: Each task uses eight student trajectories, 160 teacher-labeled macro-step contexts, and four disjoint calibration trajectories. AdamW uses learning rate 2 × 10^-5 and batch size 4 for three epochs, totaling 120 optimizer steps.
Only rank-8 JointLoRA adapters across shared Transformer blocks 0–29 are updated. Video, action, and flow-matching loss weights are respectively 1, 1, and 0.2.

Checkpoints are screened on a disjoint split using a predeclared ordering of task success, semantic progress, and calibration loss. Epoch 3 is selected for both tasks; screening data are excluded from held-out evaluation.

The package is on-policy for its released collector checkpoint only. Reusing it during updates progressively makes the training distribution stale; iterative recollection is proposed but not evaluated.

inference.text: The shared student generates and caches a video plan, then generates an action chunk from that plan and history. The deployed student executes actions and receives new observations between chunks. The pilot starts from one-video/one-action-step Flash-WAM; teacher labeling belongs to training.

equations.expression: p_θ(z_t, a_t | h_t) = p_θ(z_t | h_t) p_θ(a_t | h_t, z_t)
equations.explanation: Equation (2) expresses video-first prediction: history h_t conditions the visual future z_t, and both condition action chunk a_t. This output factorization does not imply separate networks; modality-specific interfaces surround one shared Transformer.

equations.expression: L = λ_z ρ_δ(z_S − z_T) + λ_a ρ_δ(a_S − a_T) + λ_FM ||v_θ^act(x^a_{σ=1}, 1, c) − (ε^a − a_T)||_2^2
equations.explanation: Equation (9) uses ρ_δ(e) = δ²(√(1 + (e/δ)²) − 1). Under the straight path x_σ = (1 − σ)x_0 + σε, σ = 1 is the noise boundary and ε^a − a_T is the target action velocity. Context c includes language and robot history. This endpoint-and-boundary objective is neither exact reverse KL nor full denoising-path matching.

results.task: HANDOVERMIC: transfer a microphone between robot hands
results.setting: RoboTwin 2.0 demo_clean; six held-out scene seeds × two fixed noise banks, giving 12 paired evaluation units; selected epoch-3 checkpoint.
results.metric: Official latched eval_success rate; higher is better
results.comparison: Released one-video/one-action-step Flash-WAM: 0.0%. Each comparison shares instruction, initial simulator snapshot, scene seed, and noise bank.
results.interpretation: A substantial reported gain in executed simulation task success. The two runs per scene share a seed, so the evaluation does not contain 12 independent scene samples.

results.task: PUTOBJECTCABINET: place and release an object in the designated cabinet drawer
results.setting: RoboTwin 2.0 demo_clean; six held-out scene seeds × two fixed noise banks, giving 12 paired evaluation units; selected epoch-3 checkpoint.
results.metric: Official latched eval_success rate; higher is better
results.comparison: Released one-video/one-action-step Flash-WAM: 16.7%, under the same paired evaluation protocol.
results.interpretation: The smaller improvement supports task-dependent adaptation. Drawer closing is not required by this success predicate. Results are simulation execution outcomes, not video-quality measurements or physical-robot evidence.

limitations.text: Only two clean simulation tasks and six distinct held-out scene seeds per task are tested. No uncertainty intervals accompany Table 1. Broad task generalization, domain-randomized robustness, cross-task retention, and real-robot transfer remain unestablished.
Student-side conditioning matches deployment, but teacher targets still depend on teacher video. Video alignment can reduce this discrepancy without guaranteeing exact-condition supervision.
The fixed collection package does not track the updated policy's occupancy. The pilot therefore cannot establish the value of repeatedly refreshed on-policy data.

No controlled ablation isolates student-plan conditioning, video supervision, the flow auxiliary, or shared adaptation. Shared video/action gradient interactions are unmeasured, and compute-matched SFT, RL, action-only, and full pathwise comparisons are absent.

Snapshot replay preserves poses and success-latch state but not the simulator contact manifold. Official latched success therefore does not establish sustained contact mechanics from restored-snapshot diagnostics.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires compatible LingBot-VA/Flash-WAM checkpoints, RoboTwin 2.0, the collection and evaluation partitions, replay snapshots, and fixed noise banks. The paper specifies the update schedule but leaves exact checkpoint revisions, pseudo-Huber δ, adapter target projections, and hardware/runtime unspecified.

A minimal mechanism test would fix collected histories, teacher targets, optimizer budget, checkpoint selection, and paired evaluation, then vary only whether student action training consumes z_S or z_T. A separate action-only versus joint comparison would test video supervision. Neither controlled comparison is reported.

reasoning.text: WAM and IDM are supported: generated visual futures condition inverse-dynamics action generation. The recorded Dual-system/Q4 architecture conflicts with the explicit description of modality-specific interfaces around one shared 30-block Transformer. This supports a One Model architecture assessment for the deployed student, based on shared computation rather than joint training alone. A separate frozen supervision teacher does not establish two deployed systems. The post-training and visual-planning subcategories remain supported; the recorded snapshot is preserved unchanged.

discussionQuestions: Would teacher actions conditioned directly on z_S improve supervision when student and teacher plans disagree? [e5]
At matched interaction and optimization budgets, does refreshed collection outperform the fixed package? [e8, e14]
Which loss components drive success, and does shared adaptation preserve performance on tasks outside the adaptation set? [e7, e14, e15]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The title and all four authors match the catalog. The supplied paper identifies arXiv:2608.22364v1, dated 23 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, paragraphs on covariate shift and Eq. (1)
evidence.detail: The paper distinguishes student-induced environment histories from the action-conditioning shift caused by student-generated video plans and motivates dense teacher supervision.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3, World Action Model policies, Eq. (2) and following paragraph
evidence.detail: History includes observations, prior actions, and language. Video precedes inverse-dynamics actions. Teacher and student each use modality-specific interfaces around one shared 30-block Transformer; deployment caches video before generating actions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3, Flow matching, Eqs. (3)–(5)
evidence.detail: The straight path interpolates clean data and noise; target velocity is noise minus clean data, and generation proceeds from sigma one toward zero.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, Eqs. (7)–(8) and accompanying paragraphs
evidence.detail: Student actions consume stop-gradient student video. Shared adapters remain trainable through the action pass. Teacher actions instead consume teacher video, leaving a conditional target gap.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.2, pseudo-Huber definition, Eq. (9), and weight paragraph
evidence.detail: Video/action endpoint losses and a high-noise-boundary action flow loss use weights 1, 1, and 0.2. The objective is not claimed to be exact reverse KL or full trajectory matching.
Rank-8 JointLoRA adapters cover shared blocks 0–29 while released weights are frozen. Per-modality gradient interaction is not measured.
A fixed released-student trajectory package is teacher-labeled and reused for three epochs. It becomes stale as the student changes; iterative collection is deferred.
The clean RoboTwin 2.0 tasks are microphone handover and object placement/release into a cabinet drawer. Cabinet success does not require closing the drawer.

Per task: one-video/one-action-step initialization, eight student trajectories, 160 labeled contexts, four calibration trajectories, AdamW learning rate 2 × 10^-5, batch size 4, three epochs and 120 steps. Disjoint screening selects epoch 3 for both tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.3, evaluation protocol before Table 1
evidence.detail: Six scene seeds and two noise banks produce 12 paired units per task. Paired policies share instruction, snapshot, seed and noise bank. The metric is latched eval_success; scene reuse prevents treating all units as independent scenes.
Released success is 0.0%, WAM-OPD success is 58.3%, and reported improvement is 58.3 percentage points.
Released success is 16.7%, WAM-OPD success is 33.3%, and reported improvement is 16.7 percentage points.
Broader tasks, domain randomization, action-only versus joint updates, fixed versus refreshed collection, and cross-task retention are planned; all corresponding entries are TBD.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 6, limitations preceding the final paragraph
evidence.detail: Authors acknowledge narrow simulation coverage, no real-robot evidence, stale collection, teacher/student plan mismatch, unmeasured shared-gradient interaction, and absent compute-matched alternative-training comparisons.
Snapshot restoration preserves pose and success-latch state but not contact manifolds, limiting contact diagnostics and preventing claims of verified stable contact mechanics.
